explanations.answer: They forsake the Law of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's it. Once Rehoboam's power was established, he and all Israel with him forsook the Law of the LORD (2 Chronicles 12:1). Strong throne, steady kingdom, and the Law just slides out the door. I think that's the sneaky part, friend: it happened when things were going well.

explanations.answer: They rebuild the walls of Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Close, but the text doesn't say that here. Rehoboam did build up fortified cities in Judah, but that was earlier (2 Chronicles 11:5). In 12:1 the king and all Israel with him forsook the Law of the LORD. Walls up, Law down. That's a rough trade, baker.

explanations.answer: They make a treaty with Egypt
explanations.explanation: No treaty in this passage, baker. Egypt does show up, but with an army, and we'll get to that. What verse 1 says is that Rehoboam and all Israel with him forsook the Law of the LORD. Nobody signed anything. They just walked away.

Egypt is right. Shishak is king of Egypt, and he attacks Jerusalem in Rehoboam's fifth year because they had been unfaithful to the LORD (2 Chronicles 12:2). So this army came marching up from Egypt. That's a LONG walk with chariots.

Assyria isn't in this story. The text says Shishak is the king of Egypt, and his troops come out of Egypt (2 Chronicles 12:2-3). Libyans, Sukkites and Cushites march with him. No Assyrians on the guest list, friend.

Babylon doesn't show up here, baker. Shishak is king of Egypt, and his army comes out of Egypt (2 Chronicles 12:2-3). Don't worry, I mix up directions all the time. Ask me how I found my way out of a junk drawer.

True. Shishak, king of Egypt, captured the fortified cities of Judah and came as far as Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 12:4). Those were the very kind of cities Rehoboam had built up earlier (2 Chronicles 11:5). Walls are great, but they didn't stop this army.

The text says the opposite. Shishak captured the fortified cities of Judah and came as far as Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 12:4). Rehoboam had built up cities like those earlier (2 Chronicles 11:5). So they were taken, friend, one after another.

explanations.answer: Because you left Me I have handed you over to Shishak
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Shemaiah the prophet tells them, “This is what the LORD says: ‘You have forsaken Me; therefore, I have forsaken you into the hand of Shishak.’” (2 Chronicles 12:5) It's a hard word to hear, with the army right outside the city. But the LORD tells them plainly what's going on.

explanations.answer: Stand firm and I will drive Shishak out
explanations.explanation: That's not what the LORD says here, friend. Through Shemaiah the prophet He says, “You have forsaken Me; therefore, I have forsaken you into the hand of Shishak.” (2 Chronicles 12:5) There's no promise to drive the army out in that word. It tells them why this is happening.

explanations.answer: Send gold and Shishak will turn back
explanations.explanation: No gold deal in the LORD's word. What Shemaiah the prophet says is “You have forsaken Me; therefore, I have forsaken you into the hand of Shishak.” (2 Chronicles 12:5) Nothing there about paying anybody off. You can't haggle with a prophet, baker.

Humble is right. The leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous.” (2 Chronicles 12:6) No arguing, no excuses. I tell you, friend, that takes some guts when an army is parked outside.

They didn't defend themselves, baker. The leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous.” (2 Chronicles 12:6) No speech about how it wasn't their fault. Just humble.

Nobody dives under the counter here. The leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous.” (2 Chronicles 12:6) They stood there and took the word. Hiding is what I'd have done, friend. I once hid in a drawer for years.

The text says something else, baker. After hearing the word, the king and the leaders humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous.” (2 Chronicles 12:6) That's the opposite of calling Him unfair. They agreed He was right.
False is right. The king and the leaders humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous.” (2 Chronicles 12:6) No complaining, no pointing fingers. I think that's a good sign they heard Him.

Yes, baker. When the LORD saw they had humbled themselves, He told Shemaiah, “They have humbled themselves; I will not destroy them, but will soon grant them deliverance.” (2 Chronicles 12:7) The army's still outside, but the word has changed. Humbling themselves matters.

The text says the opposite. The LORD told Shemaiah, “My wrath will not be poured out on Jerusalem through Shishak.” (2 Chronicles 12:7) Jerusalem is not going up in flames here. He also said He will not destroy them, friend.

explanations.answer: He will scatter them among the nations
explanations.explanation: Nothing about scattering in this word, baker. The LORD told Shemaiah, “They have humbled themselves; I will not destroy them, but will soon grant them deliverance.” (2 Chronicles 12:7) The people aren't being sent anywhere. They're being spared.

explanations.answer: To learn the difference between serving Him and serving other kings
explanations.explanation: That's what the LORD says. They will become Shishak's servants, “so that they may learn the difference between serving Me and serving the kings of other lands.” (2 Chronicles 12:8) So being spared from destruction doesn't mean everything goes back to normal. They're going to find out what serving other kings is like. I bet that's a lesson they remember.

explanations.answer: To give Shishak enough gold to leave the land alone forever
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different reason, baker. Shishak does take treasures later (2 Chronicles 12:9), but the LORD says they'll be servants “so that they may learn the difference between serving Me and serving the kings of other lands.” (2 Chronicles 12:8) Nobody says anything about leaving forever. The point is learning the difference.

explanations.answer: To keep Egypt from attacking the northern tribes of Israel next
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions the northern tribes here, friend. The LORD gives His reason Himself: “so that they may learn the difference between serving Me and serving the kings of other lands.” (2 Chronicles 12:8) The lesson is for Judah. Nobody is a decoy in this plan.

Bronze it is. After Shishak took the gold shields Solomon had made, King Rehoboam made bronze shields in their place (2 Chronicles 12:9-10). Solomon was David's son and Israel's king (1 Kings 2:12). The gold's gone, but the guards still have shields in their hands.

Not silver, baker. Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace the gold ones Shishak took (2 Chronicles 12:9-10). Shiny, sure, but it's bronze. Think of a cookie stamper with a dull edge: it still gets the job done.

The text says bronze, friend. After Shishak took Solomon's gold shields, King Rehoboam made bronze shields in their place (2 Chronicles 12:9-10). Solomon was David's son and Israel's king (1 Kings 2:12). Iron isn't mentioned here at all.

True. Whenever the king entered the house of the LORD, the guards would go with him, bearing the shields, and later they would return them to the guardroom (2 Chronicles 12:11). Those bronze shields had a whole routine. Walk in, walk out, back on the shelf.

The text says it's true, baker. Whenever the king entered the house of the LORD, the guards would go with him, bearing the shields, and later they would return them to the guardroom (2 Chronicles 12:11). Out they come, and back they go. That's a daily routine, friend.

Yes! Because Rehoboam humbled himself, the anger of the LORD turned away from him, and He did not destroy him completely (2 Chronicles 12:12). Humbling himself made a real difference. I love that, baker.

The text doesn't say that, friend. It says that because Rehoboam humbled himself, the anger of the LORD turned away from him, and He did not destroy him completely (2 Chronicles 12:12). Nothing about the anger being moved onto Shishak. It simply turned away from Rehoboam.

explanations.answer: It stays on all of Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The text says the anger of the LORD turned away from Rehoboam because he humbled himself (2 Chronicles 12:12). The LORD also told Shemaiah that His wrath would not be poured out on Jerusalem through Shishak (2 Chronicles 12:7). So it didn't just sit there.

Good, baker. The LORD did not destroy Rehoboam completely, and the text says, “Indeed, conditions were good in Judah.” (2 Chronicles 12:12) After an army, lost treasure and bronze shields, that's a pretty nice turnaround. Humbling yourself pays off.

Harsh would make sense after all that, but the text says otherwise. “Indeed, conditions were good in Judah.” (2 Chronicles 12:12) The LORD did not destroy Rehoboam completely. Things were going well, friend.

You'd think so after a siege, baker. But the text says, “Indeed, conditions were good in Judah.” (2 Chronicles 12:12) The LORD's anger turned away from Rehoboam. Hopeless doesn't fit that picture at all.

explanations.answer: He did not set his heart to seek the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the writer gives: “And Rehoboam did evil because he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.” (2 Chronicles 12:14) Notice that this comes right after he humbled himself and things went well. I think it shows that seeking the LORD is something you keep setting your heart to, friend. It's not a one-time thing.

explanations.answer: He trusted the gods of Egypt for protection
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, baker. The writer gives the reason plainly: “And Rehoboam did evil because he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.” (2 Chronicles 12:14) Egypt's gods aren't mentioned in this passage at all. The problem was a heart that never set itself to seek the LORD.

explanations.answer: He listened to the priests of Jeroboam
explanations.explanation: No priests of Jeroboam in this verse, friend. The writer says, “And Rehoboam did evil because he did not set his heart to seek the LORD.” (2 Chronicles 12:14) That's the whole reason given. His heart wasn't set on seeking Him.

The text says the opposite, baker. There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their days (2 Chronicles 12:15). Jeroboam was the king of Israel. So no peace treaty, no friendly neighbors, just war for as long as they both lived.

False is right. “There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their days.” (2 Chronicles 12:15) Jeroboam was the king of Israel. So even with Judah doing well, the fighting with him never ended.

Abijah is right. When Rehoboam rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David, his son Abijah reigned in his place (2 Chronicles 12:16). Rehoboam had other sons too. This one took the throne.

Jeush was one of Rehoboam's sons, baker (2 Chronicles 11:19). But the text says Abijah reigned in his place (2 Chronicles 12:16). Having the right family isn't the same as getting the crown. Abijah's the one.

Attai was one of Rehoboam's sons, friend (2 Chronicles 11:20). But the text says Abijah reigned in his place (2 Chronicles 12:16). Attai is a good name to know, but not the king. Abijah took the throne.
